content.intro: This lesson develops topic 173 of the supplied curriculum: **The base Attribute and Memory Sharing**. The main starting point is **Inspecting view relationships**. You will connect the idea to a small, synthetic example, then use the result to reason about shape, dtype, accuracy, or memory as appropriate.
content.why_it_matters: Views and references can share memory, while copies own separate data. Awareness of this difference prevents accidental mutation and helps explain memory/performance trade-offs.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Treat **The base Attribute and Memory Sharing** as an explicit step in an array workflow. This lesson centers on **Inspecting view relationships** and the source syllabus's related subtopics. Before trusting a result, identify the input shape and dtype, perform the smallest useful operation, and inspect the output. The example uses synthetic data so you can change one value and observe what changes.

content_blocks.title: Subtopics from the supplied curriculum
items: Avoiding assumptions based solely on object identity

content_blocks.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
view = a[:, :2]
print(np.shares_memory(a, view), view.base is not None)
content_blocks.expected_output:
Observed output in the available validation environment (Python 3.13.5, NumPy 2.3.5):
True True

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: `base` can provide a clue about ownership, but `np.shares_memory` is a more direct tool for checking whether two arrays overlap in memory.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a slice owns independent memory
common_mistakes.why: Basic slicing commonly creates a view.
Short timings vary due to startup, cache, and system noise.
common_mistakes.fix: Repeat measurements, use representative sizes, and compare equivalent work.
